After selecting with the predicate w greater than 5, nodes B, C, and E, whose values are 8, 6, and 9, are selected and drawn in the accent color." width="100%"} Calls a user-supplied function once for every node and selects the nodes for which it returns `True`. This is the most flexible way to build a selection: any rule that can be expressed in Python over a node's ID, label, or attributes can be used. A node selection is the input to the graph's "with selection" (`*_ws`) methods, so a typical workflow is select -> act: - tag or update a subset of nodes with `set_node_attrs_ws()` or `mutate_node_attrs_ws()` - inspect a subset as a table with `get_node_df_ws()` - prune nodes with `delete_nodes_ws()` or keep only them with `transform_to_subgraph_ws()` - use the nodes as a starting point for `trav_out()`, `trav_in()`, or `trav_both()` The matching nodes are added to the current selection, unless `set_op=` says otherwise (`"replace"`, `"intersect"`, or `"difference"`). AND/OR logic can also go in the predicate itself. The predicate runs in Python for every node, so on very large graphs the specialized selectors (e.g., `select_nodes_by_degree()`) are faster. The graph is modified in place and returned for chaining. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [predicate]{.doc-parameter-name} : A callable that receives a `Node` object and returns a `bool`. The `Node` exposes `id` (the integer node ID), `label` (the string label, or `None`), and `attributes` (a dict of the node's attributes, or `None` if the node has no attributes). Nodes for which the callable returns `True` are selected. The return value must be an actual `bool`: returning `None`, an integer, or another truthy object raises `TypeError`. Guard attribute access accordingly, e.g., `n.attributes is not None and ...` or `bool(...)`. Any exception raised by the predicate propagates, and the selection is left as it was. [set_op]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["union"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : How the matching nodes combine with the current node selection. `"union"` (default) adds them to it, `"replace"` makes them the selection, `"intersect"` keeps only the selected nodes that also match, and `"difference"` removes them from it. The graph holds a selection of nodes or of edges, never both, so any edge selection is cleared. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The same graph (modified in place) for method chaining. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [TypeError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the predicate returns something other than a `bool`. [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `set_op=` is not `"union"`, `"replace"`, `"intersect"`, or `"difference"`. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} The predicate receives each node's `Node` object, so any of its properties -- `id`, `label`, or `attributes` -- can drive the filter. Here, only "hub"-typed nodes pass, and those are the nodes with IDs `1` and `3`: ::: {#24b5a8e0 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_node(label="A", type="hub", score=10) .add_node(label="B", type="leaf", score=5) .add_node(label="C", type="hub", score=8) .select_nodes(lambda n: n.attributes.get("type") == "hub") ) sorted(graph.get_selected_node_ids()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [1, 3] ``` ::: ::: Filtering on `n.id` instead selects by internal node ID -- useful when IDs carry meaning, such as being assigned in a known order. With `set_op="replace"`, the new selection replaces the earlier one, so node `1` is no longer selected: ::: {#ebda1fc5 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.select_nodes(lambda n: n.id >= 2, set_op="replace") sorted(graph.get_selected_node_ids()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [2, 3] ``` ::: ::: With `set_op="intersect"`, a second rule narrows the selection instead. Of the nodes with IDs `2` and `3`, only "C" also has a score above `6`: ::: {#da198b46 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.select_nodes(lambda n: n.attributes["score"] > 6, set_op="intersect") [graph.get_label_from_id(nid) for nid in graph.get_selected_node_ids()] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` ['C'] ``` ::: ::: When some nodes have no attributes, `n.attributes` is `None`, so guard the lookup. The selection then feeds a `*_ws` method -- here only "B", the one node with a score above `5`, gets the new `flag` attribute: ::: {#80683747 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes([("A", {"score": 3}), ("B", {"score": 9}), "C"]) .select_nodes(lambda n: n.attributes is not None and n.attributes.get("score", 0) > 5) .set_node_attrs_ws(flag=True) ) graph.get_node_df().select("label", "score", "flag") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
